Endurance training elicits predominantly tissue-specific rather than globally coordinated molecular responses across organs. In the MoTrPAC rat multi-tissue multi-omic dataset, the mean transcriptomic Spearman correlation of training effect sizes (timewise logFC) between any two tissues is ρ = 0.10, and only 13% of tissue pairs (17/130) exceed ρ > 0.3. Mean per-assay Jaccard similarity of training-regulated feature sets ranges from 0.04 to 0.11 across molecular layers, meaning that typically only 3–11% of regulated features are shared between two tissues within the same assay.

The tissues that exhibit the most similar changes are those of shared developmental origin or physiological function:

1. Skeletal muscles (gastrocnemius and vastus lateralis) show the strongest coordination of any tissue pair: ρ = 0.73, Jaccard = 0.20, and 80% directional concordance across 218 shared genes. This coordination strengthens progressively with training duration — from ρ ≈ 0.4–0.6 at 1 week to ρ ≈ 0.88–0.91 at 8 weeks — in both sexes, suggesting that repeated training bouts progressively synchronize transcriptional programs across different skeletal muscles.

2. Brain regions (cortex and hippocampus) show coordinated responses at both transcriptomic (ρ = 0.43) and metabolomic (ρ = 0.79) levels, though the small number of shared transcriptomic features (n = 10) limits confidence.

3. Immune-related tissues (blood and spleen) exhibit moderate coordination (ρ = 0.44, Jaccard = 0.14, 338 shared genes), with a notable sex difference: female coordination is near-zero at 1 week (ρ = 0.08) but rises to strong coordination by 8 weeks (ρ = 0.71), whereas males show consistently moderate coordination across all timepoints.

4. Cardiovascular tissues (heart and vena cava) show directional concordance of 75% (ρ = 0.41), though based on only 12 shared genes.

Beyond these same-tissue-type pairs, multi-assay convergence is observed for functionally linked organ systems: heart-lung (mean ρ = 0.46 across 4 assays), kidney-lung (ρ = 0.44, 3 assays), and heart-kidney (ρ = 0.42, 4 assays), reflecting shared cardiovascular-renal-pulmonary axis responses.

In summary, endurance training does not produce a single coordinated molecular program across all organs. Instead, the response is organized into tissue-type-specific modules, with the strongest intra-module coordination between skeletal muscles — a coordination that deepens with continued training. Most cross-system tissue pairs show near-zero or weakly correlated responses, indicating that each tissue mounts its own largely independent molecular adaptation to the same systemic exercise stimulus.
